sentences: It's a gesture we make five to ten times a day, one that we were already doing in our mother's womb, and one that we share with cats, fish, and crocodiles.
A gesture so ordinary that no one thinks about it — until someone asks the question: by the way, why do we yawn?
And there, surprise: science itself has no definitive answer.
The most well-known explanation is also the most false.
We still sometimes learn it in school: we yawn to take in more oxygen into our bodies.
The idea seems logical — this big inhale, this open mouth...
Unfortunately for it, it has been tested, and it doesn't hold up.
Researchers had volunteers breathe air that was more or less rich in oxygen: the number of yawns didn't change.
The oxygen hypothesis is dead, even if it continues to circulate in conversations.
So, what are the serious leads?
The strongest one today is thermal: yawning would serve to cool the brain.
Like a computer, our brain heats up when it works, and it functions better at the right temperature.
The big jaw movement and the air inhaled would cool the blood that rises to the head.
Several observations support this: we yawn more when the temperature around us rises, and putting a cold pack on our forehead reduces the urge to yawn.
That's also why we yawn at moments of transition — waking up, falling asleep, boredom: all moments when the brain changes its state.
But the most fascinating part is the contagion.
You already know this: seeing someone yawn makes you want to yawn.
Hearing a yawn is enough.
Reading a text about yawning is enough — and I imagine you have already yawned since the beginning of this article.
This contagion is not trivial: it is linked to empathy.
Studies show that we 'catch' yawns from our loved ones more easily than those from strangers.
Young children, whose empathy is still developing, are not sensitive to it.
And your dog, after thousands of years of living with us, can catch your yawns — the only known animal to cross the species boundary in this way.
A gesture millions of years old, present before birth, contagious just by reading, and still mysterious: yawning is a beautiful lesson in humility for science.
So, how many times have you yawned while reading this?
Don't apologize.
It's proof that you are human — and probably someone empathetic.

sentences: In most major French cities, finding housing has become the main problem for residents.
Housing now accounts for about a third of a household's budget, and often much more for young people and single individuals.
How did we get here?
Several factors have added up.
First, the population of cities has increased, while the number of housing units has not kept pace.
When demand exceeds supply, prices go up: it's mechanical.
Next, the size of households has changed.
Fifty years ago, an apartment housed an average of three people; today, it's just over two.
This means more housing is needed for the same population.
Finally, in very touristy cities, part of the housing stock has shifted to short-term rentals, which are more profitable for owners.
Apartments that once housed residents now welcome travelers.
The consequences are concrete.
People who work in the city no longer live there: they move thirty or forty kilometers away and spend two hours a day commuting.
Certain essential jobs — nurses, teachers, municipal employees — are becoming hard to fill due to a lack of affordable housing.
What can be done?
No single solution is enough.
Building more is necessary, but it's slow and sometimes unpopular.
Regulating rents, as several cities do, protects tenants but doesn't create housing.
Limiting short-term rentals helps in the most affected neighborhoods.
What is certain is that this issue doesn't only concern those who are poorly housed.
A city where only the wealthiest can live will eventually lose what makes it function.

sentences: Forty years ago, people repaired things.
A toaster, a television, a washing machine: there was a repairman in every neighborhood, and replacing a working appliance would have seemed absurd.
Today, the situation has reversed.
Getting something repaired often costs almost as much as buying new, and sometimes even more.
Several reasons explain this shift.
First, the price of manufactured goods has dropped significantly, while the cost of human labor has increased.
An hour of labor can exceed the value of the appliance.
Next, the design has changed.
Many products are assembled with glue rather than screws, making them difficult to open without breaking.
Some spare parts are not sold separately, or they disappear a few years after being marketed.
Finally, software plays an increasing role.
A perfectly functional device can become unusable simply because it no longer receives updates.
However, things are changing.
France has introduced a 'repairability index' displayed on certain products, along with a repair bonus that covers part of the cost.
European law is gradually requiring the availability of spare parts.
At the same time, 'repair cafés' have emerged: volunteers help people repair things for free, teaching them to do it themselves.
I went there once with a vacuum cleaner that wasn't working.
The problem was a piece of fabric stuck in it.
The repair took twelve minutes.
I almost threw away a two hundred euro appliance.

sentences: The debate about meat is often presented in binary terms: to eat it or not eat it at all.
This opposition makes the discussion difficult, while the data suggest a more modest conclusion.
From an environmental perspective, the orders of magnitude are clear.
Livestock farming accounts for a significant portion of greenhouse gas emissions related to food, as well as considerable use of land and water.
But not all meats are equal: the gap between beef and poultry is much larger than the gap between poultry and certain plant products.
From a health standpoint, official recommendations do not call for elimination.
They advise limiting red meat and especially processed meats, without excluding other sources.
There is also a social dimension that is rarely mentioned.
Meat holds a strong symbolic place in many cultures, including in France: it marks festive meals, hospitality, and generosity.
Ignoring this leads to moralizing discourse that mainly produces resistance.

That’s why the approach that works best, in studies as well as in cafeterias, is not very spectacular: reduce frequency rather than ban, improve the quality of what is served, and offer genuinely good alternatives.
A poorly prepared vegetarian dish convinces no one.
A good vegetarian dish is chosen without thinking about it.
Personally, I have gone from eating meat almost every day to two or three times a week.
I spend the same amount because I buy better.
And I have never felt deprived.

sentences: The term 'eco-anxiety' has recently appeared in public debate.
It refers to the worry, sometimes deep, felt in response to climate change and environmental degradation.
Several international surveys indicate that a significant portion of young people report feeling anxious, and a notable fraction says it affects their daily lives, even their future plans.
We need to be cautious with these figures, but the phenomenon is real and documented.
The first thing to say is that this is not an illness.
Worrying about a documented danger is a rational reaction.
To treat this anxiety as a simple individual disorder would be to ask people to misperceive reality.
That said, anxiety that paralyzes is not helpful to anyone, neither to the person nor to the cause.
What psychologists working on this subject report is quite consistent.

What exacerbates the feeling of helplessness: the continuous consumption of catastrophic information without the possibility of acting, and isolation — experiencing this worry alone, surrounded by people who do not talk about it.
What alleviates it: concrete action, even modest, and especially collective action.

Participating in a local project, an association, or a planting initiative has a significantly greater effect than isolated individual actions, not because the impact is larger, but because one stops being alone.
Another helpful element: distinguishing what we can act on from what we cannot.
No one can solve global climate issues alone.
But almost everyone can do something somewhere, with others.

sentences: Health recommendations often mention thirty minutes of activity per day, or one hundred and fifty minutes per week.
These figures discourage many people who are far from achieving them.
However, they hide a more encouraging fact.
When we examine the relationship between physical activity and health, the curve is not straight.
The most significant benefit is not found between 'moderate' and 'intense', but between 'nothing' and 'a little'.
In other words, a completely sedentary person who starts walking for twenty minutes a day gains proportionally much more than a regular athlete who adds one more session.

It's not about reaching an ideal goal, but about moving away from zero.
A second point worth noting is that sedentariness and exercise are two distinct things.
You can run for an hour in the morning and then spend ten hours sitting.
Research suggests that prolonged sitting has its own effects, independent of physical activity.
This is why it's important to break it up: get up for a few minutes every hour, take the stairs, get off one stop earlier.
These actions do not replace sports, but they affect another factor.
Finally, the most effective activity is the one that you actually practice.
A perfect sport on paper but abandoned after a month is worth less than a daily walk maintained for ten years.
So the question is not 'what is the best exercise?'.
It is: 'what will I still be doing in a year?'

sentences: Here’s a puzzling question: a steel nail sinks immediately, but a ship weighing several thousand tons, made of the same steel, floats.
How is that possible?
The answer lies in a principle discovered in ancient times by Archimedes, and it’s simpler than it seems.
When an object is submerged in water, it pushes the water aside and takes its place.
In return, the water exerts a force on it that pushes it upward.
This force is equal to the weight of the displaced water.
An object floats if the weight of the water it displaces is greater than or equal to its own weight.
What matters is not the material itself, but the ratio between weight and volume — what we call density.
The nail is small and dense: it displaces very little water, which weighs less than it does.
It sinks.
The ship, on the other hand, is not a solid block of steel.
It’s a hull, mostly filled with air.
Its volume is enormous compared to its mass.
It therefore displaces a considerable amount of water, which weighs more than it does.
It floats.
This is also why a ship sinks further when it is loaded: it needs to displace more water to balance the extra weight.

This principle explains a multitude of everyday phenomena: why we float better in seawater, which is denser than freshwater; why a balloon filled with a light gas rises in the air, which follows the same logic.
An idea over two thousand years old continues to keep our largest ships afloat.
Science doesn’t age like techniques do.

sentences: It is often believed that good conversationalists are those who speak well, with ease and wit.
Observation suggests otherwise: it is primarily those who know how to listen.
This idea may seem obvious, but it goes against our instincts.
In a conversation, most people don't really listen: they wait for their turn.
While the other person is speaking, they are already preparing their response, looking for an anecdote to share, and waiting for the moment to jump in.
Listening becomes a pause before taking the floor again.
The people we enjoy talking to do something different.
They ask questions that extend the conversation, rather than questions that redirect it back to themselves.
They allow for silences.
Sometimes they rephrase what we've just said, which proves they have listened.
A revealing detail has been studied: after sharing an experience, there are two possible reactions.
The first brings the conversation back to oneself: 'Oh, me too, the last time...'.
The second stays focused on the other person: 'And how did you feel?'.
The first cuts the thread; the second weaves it.
This is not about forced politeness.
One can disagree, debate passionately, while still truly listening.
There is also an element of courage.
Really listening exposes you: you can be touched, contradicted, or forced to change your mind.
Speaking protects; listening opens up.
In the age of online conversations, where everyone publishes without responding to each other, this skill is becoming rare and valuable.
Next time, a simple test: count how many questions you ask about the other person.
Often, the answer is zero.

sentences: Many European cities are gradually reducing the space for cars in city centers: pedestrian streets, low-emission zones, and the removal of parking spaces in favor of bike lanes or terraces.
These decisions almost always provoke strong opposition.
It is useful to understand why and what happens next.
The expressed fears are real.
Shopkeepers fear a drop in customer numbers, convinced that their clients come by car.
Residents of the suburbs, who are less well-served by public transport, feel targeted.
Elderly people or those with reduced mobility rightly worry about accessibility.
These objections should not be brushed aside: a policy that ignores them fails and turns against itself.
However, a phenomenon repeats itself in cities that have made these changes.
First, studies show that shopkeepers generally overestimate the proportion of their customers who come by car; a majority often arrive on foot, by bike, or by public transport.
Then, once the improvements are made and the space is made pleasant, visitor numbers remain stable or even increase.
A well-designed pedestrian street attracts people.
Another recurring observation: opposition is strong beforehand, but weaker afterward.
Many residents who were initially hostile would not want to go back once they are used to it.
This does not mean that all pedestrianization is a success.
Poorly planned, without alternative transport or consideration for deliveries and accessibility, it can empty a neighborhood.
The question is therefore not 'for or against cars.'
It is: how to redistribute limited space among uses that compete for every meter?
And this question, by its nature, cannot be resolved without conflict.

sentences: We often contrast two groups: young people, who are comfortable with technology, and older adults, who feel overwhelmed.
This image contains some truth, but it's more nuanced than it seems.
It's true that older adults face more difficulties with online processes, apps, and new devices.
A significant number of them give up on services that have become exclusively digital.
This is a real problem of access to rights.
But two misconceptions need to be corrected.
The first is that young people would naturally master technology.
They know how to use apps with ease, that's true.
But using is not the same as understanding.
Many young people do not know how to assess the reliability of a source, protect their data, or fill out a complex administrative form — which requires careful reading more than dexterity.
Their ease is real in entertainment, but more fragile in other areas.
The second misconception is that age would explain everything.
In reality, the decisive factor is not just age, but exposure and necessity.
A retiree who has used a computer for work their whole life often remains comfortable; a young person without equipment at home may struggle.
What really helps to bridge this gap is not providing devices, but human support: someone patient, available, who shows without judging.
The programs that work best often rely on intergenerational connections: young people helping older adults, or the reverse for other skills.
The digital divide is therefore not a fate linked to age.
It is mainly a lack of support.
And support, unlike technology, never becomes outdated.

sentences: The scenario is repeating itself in many cities, and it has something troubling about it.
A neighborhood that was once modest, even neglected, is starting to change.
Cafés are opening, old buildings are being renovated, and wealthier residents are moving in, attracted by the charm and still affordable prices.
The neighborhood is becoming more beautiful and gaining a reputation.
And as it becomes desirable, those who have lived there forever can no longer afford to stay.
This phenomenon, often referred to by a word borrowed from English, 'gentrification', has a double face.
On one hand, it's hard to regret that a degraded neighborhood is being renovated, better maintained, safer, and better served.
Such improvements are, in themselves, welcome, and no one seriously wishes for neighborhoods to remain poor to preserve their 'authenticity'.
On the other hand, these transformations have a human cost that is too often overlooked.
As rents rise, the original residents — often the most modest — are forced to leave, driven out not by force but by price.
They are replaced without being formally evicted, which makes the injustice less visible, but no less real.
A neighborhood can thus become more beautiful while emptying of those who had made it vibrant.
What is lost is not just housing, but a web of relationships: the shopkeepers we knew, long-time neighbors, the habits patiently woven.
One does not just move out of an apartment; one is torn away from a world.
And those who arrive, however well-intentioned they may be, inherit a place whose soul has partly fled with its former inhabitants.
Should we then give up on improving poor neighborhoods?
Certainly not.
But we can do it differently, ensuring that renovations first benefit those who live there, rather than replacing them.
This requires protected housing, rent control, and a political will not to abandon residents to the sole laws of the market.
For a just city does not simply beautify its neighborhoods: it ensures that those who have inhabited them can remain.

sentences: A discreet but significant social fact marks our time: never before have so many people lived alone.
In large cities, single-person households have become one of the most common ways of life.
This phenomenon, historically unprecedented on this scale, provokes contradictory reactions: some see it as progress, while others view it as a worrying symptom.
The truth, as often, resists easy conclusions.
On one hand, living alone is also a sign of newfound freedom.
For centuries, few could afford it: people lived with family out of economic necessity, and prolonged singleness was often endured rather than chosen.
The fact that so many people can live alone today is a testament to an autonomy — material, social, personal — that did not exist before.
Many live alone because they want to, and they find a space to be fully themselves.
On the other hand, this evolution comes with a very real risk: isolation.
Living alone does not necessarily mean being alone, but the two sometimes overlap.
Without the daily connections that communal living once imposed, some slide, almost without noticing, into a solitude they did not choose.
The danger is all the greater because it is silent: one can gradually isolate themselves without anyone noticing.
We must therefore be wary of both symmetrical discourses.
Those who blissfully celebrate the solitary lifestyle forget that human beings remain social animals, who need others to thrive.
Those who lament a collapse of connection forget that living alone can be a happy choice, and that forced marriage of the past was far from paradise.
What the rise of solitary living reveals most of all is a new challenge: since we no longer live automatically surrounded, we must now build our social circles more deliberately.
The connections that communal living provided effortlessly, everyone must now cultivate: maintained friendships, vibrant neighborhoods, shared commitments.
Living alone is therefore neither a blessing nor a curse in itself; it all depends on what one makes of it, and especially on the connections one weaves beyond their own home.
Chosen solitude can be a wealth; imposed solitude remains a trial.
The whole difference lies in this little word: choose.

sentences: In the face of the scale of the ecological crisis, two opposing attitudes lead to the same result: inaction.
The first is denial, which refuses to see the problem or minimizes its severity, thus allowing nothing to change.
The second is despair, which judges the situation to be so hopeless that any effort seems futile, and it too leads to giving up.
Between these two dead ends, is there room for another attitude, a hope that is both clear-sighted and active?
Despair deserves to be taken seriously, as it is not absurd.
The news is often alarming, progress is slow, and resistance is strong.
In light of this observation, discouragement is a comprehensible reaction, and it would be futile to deny it with forced optimism.
A hope that refuses to face reality would merely be a polite form of denial.
However, despair has a decisive flaw: it is mistaken about the nature of the future.
It assumes that the worst is certain, while nothing is.
The future is not written; it depends, precisely, on what we will do.
To declare the game lost in advance is to contribute to losing it, by demobilizing those who could still act.
The paradox of despair is that it produces what it merely claims to observe.
This is where another hope becomes possible, provided we understand it well.
It is not about naively believing that everything will turn out fine, nor about reassuring oneself at little cost.
It is about recognizing that nothing is set in stone, and that this very uncertainty is a reason to act.
Since the future depends on our actions, every effort matters, not because it guarantees victory, but because it weighs on an outcome that is still open.
That hope is not a prediction; it is a choice, and almost a responsibility.
One could even say that hope, understood this way, is not a prerequisite for action, but its fruit.
It is not because we hope that we act; it is often by acting that we regain hope.
Those who engage, in their own way, almost all testify to this reversal: action, by giving meaning and control, dissipates the overwhelm that inaction maintains.
Reasonable hope is therefore neither blind optimism nor disguised resignation.
It is the conviction that, with the future remaining uncertain, it is worth fighting to influence it.
Not because we are sure to win, but because we are not sure to lose — and that is already a sufficient reason.

sentences: Modern medicine performs wonders.
It repairs severely damaged bodies, operates with incredible precision, and cures diseases that were once fatal.
This healing power is one of the great achievements of our time, and it would be ungrateful to underestimate it.
However, this medicine excels mainly at intervening once the disease has taken hold; it is much less attentive to what could prevent it from appearing.
Yet it is perhaps in prevention that the essential lies.
The idea is nothing new: it's better to prevent than to cure.
Preventing a disease from occurring is always better than having to treat it, both for the individual, spared from suffering, and for society, spared from the cost.
A considerable share of the diseases that weigh most heavily today could be avoided, or at least delayed, through lifestyle changes and early screening.
The potential for prevention is immense and largely untapped.
So why do we neglect it?
Several reasons come together.
The first relates to the very nature of prevention: its successes are invisible.
We never see the disease that never occurred, while a spectacular recovery is noticeable.
It is more gratifying, and more valued, to save a patient than to discreetly prevent them from becoming one.
Curative medicine shines; prevention works in the shadows.
The second reason is economic.
Our healthcare systems are largely organized to treat diseases, not to prevent them: we pay for the act of care much more than for the advice that would have made it unnecessary.
Prevention, lacking the same recognition, remains the poor relation of the system, despite the speeches that celebrate it.
The third reason, finally, relates to ourselves.
Preventing means acting today for a distant and uncertain benefit, which our minds, as we have seen, resist.
It is easier to put off protective efforts, even if it means having to seek treatment later.
Prevention clashes with our inclination for the immediate.
Rebalancing care and prevention does not mean giving up one for the other; both are necessary.
It is about stopping the wait for disease to act, and recognizing prevention's rightful place — in our healthcare systems as well as in our lives.
For the greatest healing is the one we never needed.

sentences: At the end of this journey through the nocturnal city, one idea emerges that connects them all: the night, with what it brings — rest, darkness, silence, a certain freedom to be unreachable — might well be something that we now need to defend as a right.
For in a world that never shuts down, that lights up, demands, and works tirelessly, what the night naturally offered is becoming rare, threatened, and must be reclaimed.
For a long time, the night imposed itself.
When darkness fell, activity ceased due to lack of light; rest followed the day as a necessity.
The night was a protected time, not by choice, but by nature.
This natural protection has disappeared.
Artificial light has abolished darkness; constant connectivity has abolished the ability to be unreachable; the demand for availability has eroded rest.
What nature guaranteed must now be desired and defended.
What is at stake goes beyond simple comfort.
Nocturnal rest is a biological necessity, as we have seen; darkness is a need for living beings; the right to be unreachable is a condition of freedom and inner life.
By allowing the night to erode, we are not losing a luxury, but fundamental needs, sacrificed to the logic of a world that wants to function without interruption.
Defending the night means defending the right to rest, to silence, to darkness, to disconnection — everything that a human being needs to recharge.
This right to the night has a social dimension, as the night is not equally accessible to everyone.

Some can protect themselves — isolate themselves from noise and light, refuse to be contacted, preserve their rest — while others endure night work, exposed housing, and the impossibility of escaping demands.
The right to the night, like the right to silence which is closely related, tends to become a privilege, reserved for those who can afford it.
Defending it also means ensuring that it is guaranteed for everyone, and not just for a few.
Defending the night requires choices, both individual and collective.
Individual: setting aside times for darkness and disconnection, protecting one's rest, resisting the pressure to always be available.
Collective: limiting light pollution, regulating night work, preserving times and spaces where the city slows down, where the night remains the night.
These choices go against a powerful logic, that of a world that wants to illuminate everything, accelerate everything, and never stop.
Recognizing a right to the night is therefore asserting a limit against this logic.

It means saying that there are moments when we need to be able to shut down, be silent, disappear, rest — and that a civilization that would abolish the night would also abolish a part of what humans need to remain human.
The night is not a void to be filled or a time to be exploited; it is a precious good that we must learn to protect again.

sentences: For most of history, the problem of truth was one of scarcity: information was hard to access, reserved for a few, and costly to obtain.
It was believed, therefore, that by making information abundant and accessible to everyone, we would bring each person closer to the truth.
This hope fueled the enthusiasm of the early days of the internet: finally, knowledge would be within everyone's reach.
However, experience has disappointed this expectation.
The problem is no longer the lack of information, but its excess — and this excess, far from bringing us closer to the truth, sometimes seems to drive us further away from it.
How can abundance harm the truth?
First, because it drowns the truth in an indistinct mass.
When information was scarce, one could hope to verify its source and weigh its value.
Today, the truth coexists with falsehood in an unending flow, with nothing distinguishing them at first glance.
In this deluge, the most blatant lie can appear the same as the most rigorous information.
Abundance does not filter; it mixes, and this mixture makes discernment more difficult, not easier.
Next, this abundance saturates our capacity for attention and judgment.
Verifying information requires time, effort, and skills; we cannot do this for the mass of information that reaches us every day.
Overwhelmed, we give up on verification, rely on impressions, and accept what comes to us without examination.
This overflow thus produces a form of cognitive laziness: the more there is to sort through, the less sorting we do.
The excess of information leads, paradoxically, to less vigilance.
There is something more serious.
In this noise, what rises to the surface is not necessarily the truth, but what captures attention: the sensational, the scandalous, what flatters our convictions or stirs our emotions.
Falsehood often has an advantage over truth: it can be designed to please, to shock, to spread, while truth, being more complex and less spectacular, spreads poorly.
In the competition for attention, truth is at a disadvantage because it was not crafted to win this competition.
Should we conclude that the abundance of information is a bad thing, and long for the scarcity of the past?
That would be excessive.
Wider access to knowledge remains a considerable progress, and many truths that were once inaccessible are now within reach.
The problem is not abundance itself, but the absence of filters, benchmarks, and skills that would allow us to find the truth.
We have gained access to everything, without acquiring the art of sorting — and it is this art that we now need to develop.
Truth, in the face of noise, no longer presents itself easily; it requires work, a method, and vigilance.
In a world of scarcity, being informed was almost enough; in a world of abundance, we must learn to discern.
This is the unique challenge of our time: no longer accessing information, but knowing how to recognize what deserves to be believed amidst the clamor.

sentences: Solitude has a bad reputation.
People avoid it, fear it, and consider it one of life's misfortunes.
Being alone is often seen as a failure, a sign that one hasn't managed to surround oneself with others, a situation to be corrected as quickly as possible.
This fear of solitude is so widespread that many cannot stand to be alone for a moment, filling every void with presence or distraction.
However, this perspective is incomplete, as it confuses two very different things: imposed solitude and chosen solitude.
Imposed solitude, that of isolation, is indeed a suffering.
Feeling alone against one's will, deprived of desired connections, excluded from the company of others, is a real ordeal, which we have seen is becoming more common.
This type of solitude must be fought against, and nothing that follows claims otherwise.
But there exists a completely different solitude: the one we choose, seek out, and make into a space for living.
And this chosen solitude, far from being a misfortune, is one of life's greatest riches.
For chosen solitude offers what the constant presence of others does not: a return to oneself.
When surrounded all the time, constantly solicited, one ends up no longer belonging to oneself, caught up in the gaze and demands of others.
Solitude is the moment when one finds oneself, when one can think without interruption, feel without having to show it, be oneself without having to deal with others.
Many essential things — deep reflection, creation, prayer, the simple rest of the mind — require this solitude and cannot be born in the continuous noise of company.
History bears witness to this fertility of solitude.
Thinkers, artists, and sages have almost all needed moments of withdrawal, away from the world, to create and to understand.
It is not a coincidence: it is in silence and solitude that the mind gathers, that ideas mature, and that one takes the necessary distance to see clearly.
Avoiding all solitude is to deprive oneself of that inner space where the deepest work takes place, the kind that no conversation can replace.
Chosen solitude also has a virtue for life with others.
Those who know how to be alone do not depend on others to avoid boredom, to feel alive, or to fill a void; they come to others by choice, not out of a need to escape their own company.
They can thus maintain freer, healthier, and less greedy relationships.
Knowing how to be alone, paradoxically, makes one better with others: we no longer ask them to save us from ourselves.
The ability to be alone is a condition for balanced relationships.
It is therefore not about choosing between others and solitude, but about making space for both.
A life entirely focused on others, without ever returning to oneself, becomes exhausted and scattered; an entirely solitary life dries up and becomes sad.
Balance lies in the alternation: moments of true connection and moments of chosen solitude.
Rehabilitating the latter, learning to be alone without suffering, to savor silence and the return to oneself, is to reclaim a part of the richness that the fear of solitude has made us forget.

sentences: In front of certain works of modern and contemporary art, a reaction often arises, so frequent that it has become almost a cliché: "it's not beautiful," "it's not art," "my child could do that."
Behind these protests lies a deep and widely shared conviction: art is meant to produce beauty, and art that breaks away from beauty betrays its vocation.
This conviction, as natural as it may seem, deserves to be questioned, because the history of modern art is precisely one of a conscious break with beauty as an end, and this break had its reasons.
First, let's recall that identifying art with beauty is neither obvious nor eternal.

For centuries, Western art did indeed aim for beauty, according to established canons; but it also aimed, and sometimes primarily aimed, at other purposes: celebrating the sacred, representing power, telling stories, edifying, commemorating.
Beauty was often a means serving these purposes, not the ultimate end.

The idea that art has only the vocation to produce beauty is itself historically situated, and questioning it does not necessarily betray art, but may reconnect with a broader conception of what art can be.
Why did modern art break with beauty?
For reasons that are not merely provocative.

First, because academic beauty, through being codified, had become an empty convention, a soulless virtuosity; breaking away from it was a way to rediscover a truth that the conventional beautiful form had ultimately stifled.

Then, because the modern world, with its horrors and upheavals, could no longer be expressed in the language of beauty alone; representing war, anxiety, the absurd required breaking harmony, for a beautiful image of horror would have been a lie.
Art that renounces beauty often seeks to express what beauty cannot say.
For art can aim for something other than aesthetic pleasure.
It can seek to provoke thought, to disturb, to reveal, to make us experience what we would prefer to ignore.
A work can be powerful without being beautiful, important without being pleasant; it can seize us with its truth, its strength, its strangeness, rather than its charm.
Reducing art to the production of beauty amputates it of these other powers, demanding that it please where it could disturb.
Art that does not seek to please is not necessarily failed art; it is sometimes art that aims higher, or elsewhere, than pleasure.
Should we then give credit to all contemporary art, and consider anyone who resists it as reactionary?
That would be to fall into the opposite excess.

For the break with beauty, while it has liberated art, has also exposed it to excesses: gratuitous provocation that says nothing, obscurity that masks emptiness, imposture that dresses itself in depth.
That art is not required to be beautiful does not mean that anything goes, nor that the absence of beauty is in itself a quality.

There is art that breaks with beauty to say more, and art that dispenses with it to have nothing to say; distinguishing them requires a judgment that neither global rejection nor blind admiration can replace.
The real question is therefore not "must art be beautiful?" which cannot be answered with a simple yes or no, but "what do we expect from art?".

If we expect only pleasure from it, then art that renounces beauty will disappoint us; if we accept that it can also make us think, disturb us, reveal us, then we can welcome works that do not seek to please.
Beauty remains one of the powers of art, one of the most precious; but making it its sole mission is to overlook all that art can be otherwise.
Art that were only beautiful would, in its own way, be as poor as art that had renounced all demands.

sentences: There are things that can be bought, and others that we believe should not be bought.
You can buy a house, but should you be able to buy a vote in elections?
You can pay for a service, but should you be able to pay for someone else to serve your prison sentence, carry your child, or give you an organ?
These questions are not economic, but moral: they concern the limits we should set on the market, on what should remain outside its reach.
And they are all the more pressing as the market today tends to expand into areas that were previously beyond its grasp.
The first argument against the unlimited expansion of the market relates to inequality.
Where everything is for sale, those who have money obtain what others cannot have; wealth inequality then translates into inequality of access to everything that matters.

As long as the market is limited to consumer goods, this inequality is bearable; but if it extends to health, justice, education, and political influence, it transforms economic inequality into inequality regarding the most essential goods.
The more the market expands, the more money becomes decisive, and the greater the impact of wealth inequalities on all aspects of existence.
Limiting the market means preventing wealth from buying everything.
But there is a second, deeper argument that does not concern inequality but the very nature of certain goods.
For putting something on the market, giving it a price, can corrupt it, distort it, and cause it to lose its intrinsic value.

Some things are valuable precisely because they cannot be bought: friendship that could be bought would no longer be friendship, honor that could be sold would no longer be honor, and the price of a reward that could be purchased would strip it of its meaning.
There are goods whose value lies in the fact that they are given, earned, received, and not bought; subjecting them to the market does not make them accessible, it destroys them as what they were.
This second argument is decisive, as it shows that the question of the limits of the market is not just a question of distributive justice, but a question about the meaning and value of things.

When we refuse to allow certain things to be bought, it is not only because it would be unequal; it is because buying them would distort them, substituting the only measure of money for their intrinsic value.

A society where everything could be bought would not only be more unequal; it would be a society where nothing would have value beyond its price, where everything would be reduced to its market value, and where the very meaning of goods that cannot be reduced to money would be lost.

That is why the question of the limits of the market is one of the most important of our time, where the market tends to overflow its traditional boundaries, to put a price on what did not have one, and to treat as commodities things that were not.
This expansion often presents itself as progress, efficiency, and freedom; but it silently operates a transformation of our values, making the market the measure of all things.

Resisting this expansion is not opposing the market in its legitimate domain, where it provides immense services; it is refusing to let it become the sole principle of organization for all human life.
Drawing the limits of the market is not a task that economics could accomplish, as it is a moral task that engages our conception of what has a price and what has a value beyond any price.
It requires us to ask, for each good, whether it can be bought and sold without harm, or if its nature demands that it escape the market.
This deliberation, never closed, is one of the responsibilities of a society that does not want to be entirely governed by money.

For the real question is not whether money can, in fact, buy everything — it increasingly can — but whether there are things it should not be able to buy, if we want to preserve what is worth more than its price in human existence.

sentences: Be yourself," "stay true to yourself," "be authentic": these injunctions have become self-evident in our time, ideals that no one thinks to contest.
Being authentic, true to one's deep self, opposed to conformity and social lies, is seen as the hallmark of a successful life.

However, this ideal, as appealing as it may be, rests on assumptions that need to be examined, because it presupposes as resolved what is precisely problematic: the existence of an authentic self, already given, to which one should be faithful.

The ideal of authenticity indeed assumes that there exists, deep down in each of us, a true self, a proper nature, an authentic identity that would be our truth, as opposed to the masks we wear in society.
Being true to oneself would then mean discovering this deep self and conforming to it, against the pressures that lead us away from it.
But this image assumes that the authentic self preexists, that it is there to be discovered, like a buried treasure.
Yet we have seen that the self may not be a fixed thing, predetermined, but something that is constructed.
If that is the case, to which already existing self should one be faithful?
There is something more troubling.
The ideal of authenticity opposes the deep, authentic self to external, social influences that would lead us astray.
But is this opposition tenable?
Isn't what we call our deep self also largely the product of influences—our education, our culture, our environment, others?
What I take to be my authentic nature may be what I have received unknowingly, internalized to the point of believing it is mine.
The idea of an authentic self, free from any social influence, may be an illusion: there is no self that would preexist influences, because we are woven from them.
To want to be true to a self prior to any influence is to pursue a ghost.
Should we then reject the ideal of authenticity, seeing it as a pure illusion?
That would be too hasty, as it expresses a real and legitimate aspiration.
What it aims for, under a questionable formulation, is the rejection of alienation, of false living, of submission to the gaze of others that we have mentioned.

Being authentic, properly understood, may not be about being true to a given self, but about refusing to live in contradiction with what one believes, what one wants, what one judges to be good; it is not to renounce oneself, not to betray oneself, not to live a life that would not be one's own.
Authenticity as coherence, as a refusal of self-deception, retains all its meaning even if the 'authentic self' as a fixed thing is an illusion.
This reformulation changes everything.

If authenticity is not fidelity to a given self, but coherence between what one does and what one believes, then it is not the discovery of a nature, but a moral requirement, a way of conducting oneself.
Being true to oneself is not about exhuming a buried treasure; it is about building a coherent existence, taking responsibility for one's choices, and not living in contradiction with one's values.
The self to which one is faithful is not a prior given, but a work in progress, which fidelity itself helps to shape.
One does not find one's self; one makes it, striving not to betray it.

The ideal of authenticity, thus understood, ceases to be the impossible injunction to discover a hidden self, and becomes the difficult but sensible requirement to lead a coherent and non-alienated life.
It is not about digging within oneself to find one's truth, but about living in such a way that one can recognize oneself in what one does, not lying to oneself, not betraying oneself.
This kind of authenticity is not given; it is earned, through the effort to align one's life with one's convictions.
"Be yourself" therefore does not mean "conform to what you already are," but rather "make sure to become someone you won't be ashamed of"—which is a task, not a discovery.

sentences: There seems to be, in human beings, a need for transcendence: the need to go beyond the everyday, to connect with something greater than oneself, to find a meaning that exceeds ordinary existence.
This need was long fulfilled by religion, which offered an afterlife, an absolute, a communion with the divine.
The decline of traditional religions in our societies raises a question: has this need for transcendence disappeared along with the beliefs that satisfied it, or does it persist, seeking new outlets?
The answer reveals a lot about our condition.
One hypothesis suggests that this need was an illusion, a product of ignorance and fear, which the progress of reason would have dispelled.
Freed from religious beliefs, we would no longer need transcendence, contenting ourselves with the world as it is, without an afterlife or beyond.
This hypothesis is coherent, but it runs into a stubborn fact: the need for transcendence does not seem to have disappeared with the religions that fulfilled it.
Secularized societies manifest, in other forms, a persistent quest for transcendence, meaning, and the absolute, suggesting that this need is deeper than a mere dated belief.
For this need, stripped of its traditional religious forms, seems to shift to other objects.

We find it in the quest for meaning that runs through our societies, in the aspiration for experiences that surpass us, in the renewed forms of spirituality that flourish outside established religions, in the almost religious investment in causes, ideals, and sometimes idols.
We find it in art, which offers a form of secular transcendence, in nature, where many seek the feeling of surpassing, in the commitment to causes that give existence a meaning that exceeds it.
The need for transcendence has not disappeared; it has shifted, seeking outside of religion what it once offered.
This shift is not without ambiguity.
Some of these substitute transcendences are fruitful, offering authentic meaning and surpassing without religious dogmas.
But others are more troubling, even dangerous: the need for transcendence, deprived of legitimate objects, can shift to harmful idols, fanatical causes, and murderous absolutes.
History shows that societies that have repressed the sacred have sometimes seen the need for transcendence resurface in terrible political forms, secular religions that have shed blood.
The need for transcendence, when it does not find healthy objects, can invest in destructive ones.
What to make of this observation?
It first invites us to recognize this need rather than deny it.

To claim that modern man no longer needs transcendence, that he would be satisfied with a purely immanent, calculating, material existence, is to overlook a profound dimension of the human condition and risk seeing it resurface in uncontrolled forms.
A society that makes no room for the need for surpassing, that reduces existence to consumption and calculation, may be preparing for the wild return of what it has repressed.
Recognizing the need for transcendence is to give ourselves a chance to offer it worthy objects rather than letting it invest in idols.
It is not about advocating a return of religions, nor about settling the question of their truth.

It is about recognizing that the need to go beyond the everyday, to connect with something greater than oneself, to find a meaning that exceeds ordinary existence, is a lasting dimension of humanity that secularization has not abolished.
Understanding this is to guard against both the materialism that denies this need and allows it to resurface in bad forms, and the fanaticism that fulfills it with destructive absolutes.

Between the two, we need to invent forms of transcendence that respond to this need without enslaving it: in art, thought, commitment, contemplation, everything that elevates man above himself without delivering him to idols.
For this need cannot be eliminated; we can only offer it worthy objects or let it find harmful ones.

sentences: Today, curiosity enjoys unanimous prestige: it is regarded as a virtue, a quality to cultivate, the driving force behind learning and discovery.
Children are encouraged to be curious, curious minds are celebrated, and a lack of curiosity is lamented as a flaw.
However, it hasn't always been this way.
For centuries, curiosity was viewed with suspicion, even condemned as a vice, a dangerous passion.
This reversal, from vice to virtue, deserves to be examined, as it reveals a profound transformation in our relationship with knowledge and the desire to know.
Why was curiosity long considered suspect?
Several reasons came together.
It was first seen as a form of excess, the desire to know what one should not, to cross the boundaries assigned to human knowledge, to uncover reserved secrets.
Curiosity was the desire to know what does not concern us, to venture where man should not go; it had something of transgression, of the pride in wanting to know everything.

It was also seen as a dispersion, an inconsistency of the mind that scatters according to its desires, shows interest in everything without delving deeply into anything, and chases novelty without settling down.
Curiosity, in this sense, opposed wisdom, which knows how to limit its desire for knowledge and focus on the essentials.
The reversal that made curiosity a virtue stems from modernity, particularly from the rise of science.
For modern science has precisely made the desire to know, the will to uncover the secrets of nature, and the audacity to question what was believed to be forbidden, the driving force of its approach.
What was condemned as excess — wanting to know everything, crossing boundaries, uncovering secrets — has become the spring of scientific progress.
Curiosity, which was once a vice, has become the quintessential virtue of the scientific mind, the disposition that drives one to seek, to discover, and to be unsatisfied with any ignorance.
The reversal of its value accompanies the advent of a civilization based on knowledge and progress.
This reversal reflects a transformation in our relationship with the limits of knowledge.

Where it was once considered wise to limit one's desire to know, to respect boundaries, and not to want to know everything, modernity has made the unlimited pursuit of knowledge an ideal: there would be no forbidden knowledge, no legitimate limit to curiosity, everything would deserve to be known.
This conception has allowed for immense progress by freeing the desire to know from any hindrance.
But it does raise questions: is there really no legitimate limit to curiosity?
Are some forms of knowledge not dangerous, are there not certain secrets that are better left undiscovered?
Curiosity elevated to an absolute virtue ignores these questions, which ancient suspicion, for other reasons, raised.
Perhaps the truth is that curiosity is neither simply a vice nor simply a virtue, but an ambivalent power, depending on its object and its measure.

There is a fruitful curiosity that drives one to understand, to discover, to open up to the world, and which is indeed a virtue; and there is a vain or unhealthy curiosity that scatters, clings to what is not worthy, violates the intimacy of others, or ventures where it causes harm.
The curiosity that deepens differs from that which flits about; the one that seeks the truth differs from the one that feeds on scandal.
To judge curiosity as a whole, as either a vice or a virtue, is to miss this distinction: it all depends on what it is directed towards and the measure it maintains.
The reversal of the value of curiosity thus teaches us something about ourselves.
It reveals that we have made the desire to know an absolute, that we have lifted the old suspicions, and that we take for granted a valuation that was not self-evident.

Recognizing this reversal does not advocate a return to ancient condemnation, but rather regaining a part of our clarity: to ask whether there really is no limit to curiosity, to distinguish fruitful curiosity from that which is not, and not to elevate the desire to know everything to an unqualified virtue.
Curiosity is a magnificent power; but every power, to be a virtue, needs to be directed and measured.
Wisdom may not be to condemn it or to celebrate it unreservedly, but to learn how to make good use of it.
Our time has made memory a virtue and forgetting a vice.
To remember would be a duty, forgetting a fault, even complicity.
This one-sided valorization of memory, so understandable after centuries where crimes were buried in silence, deserves to be nuanced.
For forgetting, which we condemn, also has its functions and necessities; a society that could not forget anything would not be more just, but perhaps more imprisoned by its past.
We must have the audacity to ask ourselves if forgetting, within certain limits, is not also necessary.
Let's first consider the individual.
A memory that would know no forgetting would be an unbearable burden.
To remember everything, to relive every offense, every suffering, every wound endlessly, would prevent one from living: one would be crushed under the weight of a past that would never pass.
For the individual, forgetting is not just a failure of memory; it is a vital function that lightens, that allows one to turn the page, to heal, to move forward.
He who can forget nothing, who endlessly ruminates on his grievances, condemns himself to perpetual suffering.
Forgiving, reconciling, starting over requires a form of forgetting, or at least a calming of memory.
What applies to the individual also partly applies to societies.
After great rifts — civil wars, fratricidal conflicts — peoples have often had to consent to a form of forgetting in order to rebuild.
Not the erasure of facts, but the renunciation of vengeance, of the perpetual rehashing of wrongs, of the rekindling of hatreds.
Some exits from conflict have relied on amnesties, pacts of forgetting, which allowed former enemies to live together again.
These forgettings were not betrayals of memory; they were the condition for a peace without which memory would have only perpetuated war.
A society that would never forget any of its fractures would constantly reopen them.
There is a paradox here that must be acknowledged.
On one hand, forgetting crimes is an injustice, and the duty of memory is right to combat it.
On the other hand, the impossibility of forgetting traps one in the past, fuels hatreds, and forbids reconciliation.
How can we reconcile these two truths?
Perhaps by distinguishing the objects and moments of forgetting.

There are things that must not be forgotten — the facts, the victims, the responsibility for crimes; and others that must be allowed to calm — the thirst for vengeance, resentment, the desire for endless retribution.
Remembering the facts does not obligate one to maintain hatred; one can keep memory alive and lay down the arms of resentment.
This distinction sheds light on what a balanced relationship with the past could be.
Neither the forgetting that erases and prepares for repetition, nor the memory that rehashes and perpetuates war, but a calm memory that knows the facts without turning them into an eternal weapon.
Forgiveness, which is so often discussed, is not the forgetting of facts; it is the renunciation of vengeance despite the memory.
This may be the highest form of relationship to the past: to remember fully, and yet cease to make memory a motive for hatred.
Not forgetting to forgive, but forgiving without forgetting.
Rehabilitating a part of forgetting is therefore not betraying memory; it is recognizing that memory alone is not enough, and that it can even, if misdirected, become a poison.
A society, like a human being, needs both to remember and to be able to let the past pass; otherwise, it remains imprisoned by its wounds.
Wisdom, here as elsewhere, is not in one term against the other, but in their just balance: knowing what must be kept alive, and what must be allowed to calm.
For a people that would never forget anything would be as unhappy as a people that had forgotten everything.

sentences: We live with the feeling that civilization is a solid achievement, an irreversible progress that has definitively pulled us away from barbarism.
Our institutions, our laws, our softened morals, and our horror of cruelty seem to us like assured conquests, a foundation we can rely on.
However, this confidence may rest on an illusion.
For what we call civilization might well be nothing more than a fragile veneer, a thin layer covering older and darker forces that can crack and unravel with disconcerting speed.
This unsettling truth has been demonstrated by history too often to be ignored.
The twentieth century, in particular, dealt a brutal blow to the idea of a civilization that is definitively acquired.

Some of the most advanced, cultured, and refined societies plunged into a barbarism that was thought to be a thing of the past within just a few years, committing or tolerating atrocities of unprecedented scale.
This shift did not come from peoples who remained savage, but from nations at the pinnacle of culture, science, and refinement.

It showed that the veneer of civilization could crack, that beneath the softened morals lay forces that circumstances could awaken, and that the civilized man and the barbarian were not two distinct species, but that the latter could resurface within the former with frightening ease.
How can we understand this fragility?
Perhaps by recognizing that civilization does not fundamentally transform human nature, but contains it, channels it, and represses it.

The impulses of violence, cruelty, and domination do not disappear under the influence of civilization; they are contained by institutions, prohibitions, customs, and education, which repress and subliminate them.
But these barriers are fragile; if they give way, due to a crisis, propaganda, or a collapse, the forces they contained can resurface.
Civilization would not be the abolition of barbarism, but its precarious containment, always threatened with rupture.
This conception, as bleak as it may be, has the merit of lucidity.
It protects us from two dangerous illusions.

The first is the naive optimism that believes civilization is permanently secured, that barbarism is a thing of the past, and that progress is irreversible; this optimism disarms, as it does not see the danger approaching, and it does not defend what it believes is assured.

The second is to believe that barbarism is the fault of others, of peoples who remain savage, and that we, the civilized, are forever preserved from it; this illusion blinds us to our own capacity to fall, to the forces that our civilization contains without abolishing them.
Recognizing the fragility of civilization means guarding against these blind spots, and thus defending it better.
For this clarity leads to a requirement: if civilization is fragile, then it must be constantly defended, maintained, and protected.
It is not an achievement that one can enjoy passively, but a conquest that must always be reclaimed, a balance that is always threatened, and dikes that must be constantly reinforced.

The institutions that contain violence, the customs that soften, the education that civilizes, the prohibitions that protect, only hold if we maintain them, if we watch over them, if we do not let them deteriorate.
Civilization does not maintain itself; it requires constant effort, vigilance from each generation, without which it can unravel.
Recognizing that civilization is a fragile veneer is therefore not yielding to pessimism or despair.
It is to gain the clarity that alone allows us to defend it.
He who believes civilization is secured does not defend it and lets it deteriorate; he who knows its fragility watches over it, protects it, and transmits it.

The awareness of fragility is not demobilizing but mobilizing: it reminds us that what we hold most precious — peace, rights, the gentleness of customs, the horror of cruelty — is never definitively secured, that it must be earned and defended in every generation, and that it can be lost if we cease to watch over it.
Civilization is a fragile heritage; and it is because it is fragile that it obliges us — to take care of it, to transmit it, to never take it for granted.
For what centuries have built, a few years can undo; and it is up to us, in each generation, to ensure that the veneer does not crack.

sentences: We spontaneously regard death as the great evil, which deprives us of life, against which we rebel.
And yet, a troubling question deserves to be asked: could death, our finitude, paradoxically be what gives life some of its meaning and value?
Would a life without end, immortal, be richer, or would it instead lose what gives existence its worth?
This question, which seems to go against our deepest desire — that of not dying — may reveal an unexpected link between finitude and meaning.
Let’s reflect on what an immortal life would be like.
An existence without end, where time would never be counted, where nothing would ever be urgent, where everything could always be postponed indefinitely.

In such an existence, each moment would lose its unique and irreplaceable character; since time would be infinite, no moment would have particular value, no opportunity would be worth seizing, no choice would be decisive.
Unlimited time would lose its value, just as what is available without limit loses its value.
What gives time its worth is precisely that it is counted; an immortal life, by abolishing this rarity, might abolish what gives time, and life, their value.
There’s more.
It’s because our time is limited that we make choices, that we commit ourselves, and that our decisions carry weight.

In the face of infinite time, no choice would truly be necessary, since we could always do anything, try everything, and postpone everything; commitment, which involves giving up other possibilities to realize one, would lose its meaning, since nothing would force us to renounce.

Finitude is what gives our choices their gravity, our commitments their weight, and our lives their shape; for it is because we cannot do everything, experience everything, or be everything that we must choose, and these choices define us.
An infinite life would be a life without form, without decisive choices, without true commitment.
We can go even further.
It may be the awareness of death that makes possible the very intensity of life, love, beauty, everything that touches us.
We love intensely what we know we must lose; we fully savor what we know is ephemeral; the awareness of finitude gives what we experience an intensity that eternity would take away.
Would an eternal love, assured never to end, have the same intensity as a love threatened by death?
Would an eternal beauty touch us like one that we know is fleeting?
It could be that the intensity of life is linked to its finitude, that it is because everything passes that everything touches us, and that eternity, by abolishing loss, would also abolish intensity.
Should we conclude that we ought to rejoice in death, desire it, and see it as a good thing?
That would be going too far and betraying our experience.
For death remains, in many ways, an evil: it deprives us of life, tears us away from those we love, and puts an end to what is dear to us.
Recognizing that finitude gives meaning to life does not mean denying that death is a loss, a pain, a tearing apart.
The truth is more nuanced: death is both an evil, which deprives us, and a condition of meaning, which gives life its value.
It is ambivalent, like finitude itself: what limits us and what constitutes us, what deprives us and what gives value to what we enjoy.
This ambivalence may be the deepest truth about our mortal condition.
We can neither purely rejoice in death, which remains a loss, nor absolutely curse it, for it is also a condition of meaning.

Wisdom may consist in holding both: recognizing death as an evil, while continuing to fight it where we can, and at the same time recognizing that finitude gives life its value, that it is because we are mortal that our lives have a form, an intensity, a meaning.
Not to love death, but to accept finitude; not to desire immortality, which would abolish meaning, but to fully live a life that its very finitude makes precious.
Death does not give meaning to life as an answer; but our finitude is the condition that makes meaning possible, by giving our lives the form, intensity, and gravity that eternity would take away.

And perhaps it is in this that, without ceasing to be an evil, death contributes to what makes life something other than an indefinite duration: an existence that, because it ends, deserves to be fully lived.

sentences: In December, I failed my first exam at university, a math exam.
I thought I had worked well, but I didn't understand how to study effectively at this level.
When I saw my grade, I was shocked.
I had never failed an exam in high school.
My first reaction was to feel worthless, unable to succeed in my studies.
The next day, I decided to go talk to my professor, despite my embarrassment.
He was very understanding.
"Many students fail their first exam here, he told me.
It's a new system, it takes time to adapt."
He explained to me that the study method in high school was not enough for university.
You had to work regularly, not just before the exam.
He advised me to join a study group with other students.
I followed his advice, and I completely changed my way of working.
In the second exam, in May, I got a much better grade.
This failure, as difficult as it was at the time, taught me how to study better.

sentences: A three-euro t-shirt: how is that even possible?
I recently asked myself this question in a store where the prices seemed almost unreal.
Three euros normally doesn't even cover the cost of the fabric, transportation, and manufacturing.
In trying to understand, I discovered a complex chain: cotton grown in one country, woven in another, sewn in a third, before finally arriving in our stores.
At each stage, someone gets paid, but often very little.
The workers who sew these clothes sometimes earn the equivalent of just a few cents per piece.

There is also a significant environmental cost, rarely visible on the label: the water needed to grow cotton, the chemicals used for dyeing, and finally, the millions of clothes thrown away each year after only a few uses.
Some certifications, meant to guarantee decent working conditions, are in practice difficult to verify: brands are happy to talk about their efforts, much less about their exact suppliers.
A friend who works in textile auditing confessed to me one evening that he only trusts a handful of labels on an entire shelf.
Given these figures, it's hard to keep buying without thinking about it, at least for me.
I'm not saying we should stop buying new clothes; that would be naive and unrealistic for most people.
But maybe we should ask ourselves, before each very cheap purchase, who has really paid the difference.

sentences: One Sunday, I suggested to my parents that we watch a movie together that I loved, a recent work with fast editing and a non-linear narrative.
After twenty minutes, my father paused it.
"I don't understand anything about this story," he admitted.
"It's going too fast, and it jumps from one moment to another without warning."
My mother, on the other hand, found the movie "stressful," as the images changed quickly on the screen.
This experience made me think about how each generation learns, almost unconsciously, a certain cinematic language.
Used to fast editing and non-chronological storytelling since childhood, younger viewers naturally decipher what my parents found confusing.
In contrast, when my parents introduce me to an older film, with a slow and steady pace, I sometimes struggle to stay focused, being used to a more dynamic narrative.
So it's not just a matter of taste, but also a matter of perceptual habit, shaped by what each generation has watched the most.

Since that missed evening, we have gotten into the habit of switching roles: I choose a movie that my parents would have liked at the same age, while they try, on their side, to understand what attracts me to my own choices.
The result is usually awkward, but something gets a little closer.
This discovery has made me more understanding towards both generations: neither my parents nor I are "wrong" in the way we watch a film.
We have simply learned, each in our own time, a different visual language.

sentences: Sports doping is often presented as a recent problem, linked to the excesses of contemporary professional sports and the financial pressure that comes with it.
History, however, tells a very different story: the temptation to artificially enhance performance has accompanied competitive sports since its earliest origins.
As early as Antiquity, some Greek athletes were already consuming plant or mushroom-based preparations in the hope of increasing their strength or endurance before a competition.
These practices, although rudimentary compared to modern chemical substances, were based on exactly the same logic: seeking a competitive advantage beyond the natural limits of the body.
What has truly changed over time is the increasing sophistication of methods, as well as the much more recent ability to detect them scientifically.

The major scandals of the twentieth century did not reveal the emergence of doping, but rather the new means to uncover it, in a context where the economic stakes of professional sports had significantly increased.
This historical perspective invites us to nuance a discourse that can sometimes be overly moralistic, which would present doping as a simple individual deviance specific to our time.
The phenomenon seems rather inseparable from competition itself, as long as victory provides a sufficiently significant advantage, whether material or symbolic, to justify taking a risk.
This obviously does not mean that we should give up the fight against doping, whose health consequences and impact on sports fairness remain very real.

But understanding its historical depth may allow us to approach this struggle with greater clarity: not as the eradication of an isolated modern evil, but as the constant regulation of a temptation as old as human competition itself.

sentences: Many studies today demonstrate that teenagers have a biological rhythm that is naturally shifted compared to adults, causing them to fall asleep and wake up later, a phenomenon directly linked to the hormonal changes typical of this stage of life.

Despite these well-established scientific findings, the majority of schools continue to impose early start times for classes, historically designed according to the constraints of adults rather than the actual biological needs of the teenagers themselves.

This contradiction produces widely documented concrete consequences: drowsiness in class, difficulties concentrating during the first classes of the day, and a chronic sleep deficit that accumulates throughout the school week, rarely compensated for sufficiently on the weekend.
In light of this observation, several institutions, particularly in the United States and in some Scandinavian countries, have begun to experiment with class start times delayed by about an hour.
The initial results of these experiments show measurable improvements: better concentration, reduced absenteeism, and even a decrease in road accidents among young drivers heading to school.

However, the obstacles to generalizing these measures remain numerous: organization of school transport, constraints of parents working fixed hours, extracurricular activities scheduled at the end of the day.

These very real practical difficulties largely explain the slow pace at which educational systems adapt their schedules to scientific knowledge that has been well established for several years already.

sentences: For the first time in human history, a significant part of what we experience is recorded, not by our fallible and selective biological memory, but by digital devices of remarkable fidelity, which effortlessly and indiscriminately preserve photographs, messages, locations, entire conversations, in a completeness that no human memory has ever been able to approach.

This massive externalization of memory, which at first glance seems like a welcome prosthesis compensating for the very real shortcomings of our biological memory, deserves a closer examination of its consequences on the very construction of personal identity.

For if we accept, as contemporary analysis of memory suggests, that memory is never a simple faithful recall but an active reconstruction, shaped by who we become, then a perfectly faithful digital memory, refusing all forgetting and all reconstruction, comes into direct tension with the process by which an individual, precisely, constructs and reinvents themselves over time.

Let’s consider what happens when a digital photograph, taken ten years earlier, resurfaces in an automatic notification, showing a version of ourselves that our own more lenient memory had long since reinterpreted, softened, or simply allowed to fade.

This confrontation between lived memory, subjective and evolving, and digital recording, literal and fixed, produces a particular dissonance: we suddenly find ourselves confronted, not with our own reconstruction of the past, but with a version of that past that we did not choose to preserve in this way, and which is nonetheless presented to us with the indisputable authority of a document.

This unprecedented situation raises a philosophical question whose implications go beyond simple technological nostalgia: which, of the reconstructive and living biological memory, or the faithful and fixed digital archive, holds the legitimate authority over what we were?

Traditionally, the individual remained the sole custodian, and the sole judge, of what they chose to retain from their own past, operating this largely unconscious selection that allowed them to construct a coherent, bearable, evolving narrative of self.

Digital memory, by imposing its own version, literal and uncompromising, of the past, potentially deprives the individual of this ancient prerogative: that of deciding, at least in part, what their own past should mean for them today.
This situation affects different generations currently living in unequal ways.

Those who reached adulthood before the advent of this widespread digital memory have a radically different relationship to their own past than those generations born into a world where every moment, from birth, is potentially documented, indexed, and indefinitely preserved by third parties.

No one yet knows precisely what it means, for the construction of personal identity, to grow up knowing that one's entire childhood remains accessible, in every detail, to oneself as well as to others, without the relative protection that once offered the natural and gradual forgetting of those distant years.

It would be tempting to say that there is no obligation to consult these digital archives, and that their mere existence, somewhere on a distant server, does not in itself impose a constraint on the individual who could, in principle, completely ignore them.

However, this response overlooks the concrete reality of contemporary exposure to these devices, whose automatic notifications, algorithmic reminders, and unsolicited resurgences often impose themselves without the user having actively sought them out, or even anticipated them.

Perhaps we should then consider, in light of this new configuration, a form of voluntary discipline to cultivate: not to outright reject these memory technologies, which have considerable practical utility, but to reclaim, at least partially, this ancient prerogative of selection and reconstruction that has always characterized living human memory, by resisting the temptation to let the digital archive, in its blind and nuanced fidelity, dictate alone what our own past should now mean to us.

sentences: Small businesses in the city center are seeking a new balance.
For several years, they have been facing competition from online shopping, rising commercial rents, and changing habits.
Many residents still walk past the shop windows, but they buy less often on-site.

A bookstore organizes meetings with authors.
A clothing store offers quick alterations.
A wine merchant hosts discovery evenings to attract customers who wouldn't have come just to buy a bottle.
The town hall is also trying to take action.
It funds Saturday events and helps shops improve their online presence.

It raises a very current question: what do we want to find in the center of a city?

sentences: At seventy-two years old, my mother bought a tablet.
She wanted to see her grandchildren on video because they live far away.
I offered to teach her.
I thought it would be quick.
I was completely mistaken.
On the first day, we spent two hours on things I thought were obvious.
How to turn on the device.
How to touch the screen, not too hard and not for too long.
I realized that I wasn't explaining well.
I was using words like 'app' or 'menu' without defining them.
For me, it was natural; for her, it was a foreign language.
I also noticed something else: she was afraid.
Afraid of clicking in the wrong place, of breaking everything.
So I told her a phrase that helped a lot: 'You can't break anything.
If you make a mistake, we'll fix it in thirty seconds.'
After that, she dared to try on her own.
We did something useful: we wrote a little notebook.
At each step, she wrote down the instructions in her own words.
This notebook is still useful to her.
It took about two months.
Today, she calls her grandchildren on video by herself, she sends photos, and she reads the newspaper online.
Last week, she called me to show me something I didn't know how to do.
