The hills, which rose behind the coast, were crowned with green trees, among which the pine predominated.
These were significant clusters of these resinous species, which could be referred to as forests in certain places.
Sometimes, in isolated groups, Jasper Hobson noticed willows, poplars, dwarf birches, and numerous arbutus bushes.
At this time of the warm season, all these trees were lush, and they somewhat surprised the eye, accustomed to the stark and bare profiles of polar landscapes.
The ground at the foot of the hills was covered with short grass, which the reindeer grazed eagerly, and which was meant to nourish them during the winter.
As we can see, the lieutenant could only be pleased to have sought out in the northwest of the American continent a new area for exploitation.
It has also been said that while animals were not lacking in this territory, men seemed to be completely absent.
Neither Eskimos, whose tribes prefer to roam the areas closer to Hudson Bay, nor Indians, who do not usually venture this far beyond the Arctic Circle, were seen.
Indeed, at this distance, hunters can be caught in continuous bad weather, by a sudden return of winter, and then be cut off from all communication.
It is clear that Lieutenant Hobson did not think to complain about the absence of his fellow men.
He could only have found rivals among them.

It was an unoccupied land he was seeking, a desert where fur-bearing animals would likely seek refuge, and in this regard, Jasper Hobson had the most sensible remarks for Mrs. Paulina Barnett, who was very interested in the success of the venture.

So you see that sodium chloride is present in a notable proportion.
Now, it is this sodium that I extract from seawater and use to compose my elements.
-- Sodium?
-- Yes, sir.
Mixed with mercury, it forms an amalgam that serves as zinc in the Bunzen elements.
Mercury never wears out.
Only sodium gets consumed, and the sea provides it for me.
I will also tell you that sodium batteries should be considered the most powerful, and their electromotive force is double that of zinc batteries.
I understand well, captain, the value of sodium in the conditions you find yourself in.
The sea contains it.
Good.
But it still needs to be manufactured, extracted in a word.
And how do you do that?
Your batteries could obviously be used for this extraction; but, if I'm not mistaken, the sodium consumption required by the electrical devices would exceed the amount extracted.
So it would happen that you would consume more to produce it than you would actually produce!
-- So, professor, I don't extract it using the battery, and I simply use the heat from coal.
-- From coal? I said, insisting.
Let's say sea coal, if you prefer, replied Captain Nemo.

sentences: Calypso, who had until that moment been motionless and filled with delight listening to the adventures of Télémaque, interrupted him to suggest he take some rest.
It is time, she said to him, for you to enjoy the sweetness of sleep after so much work.
You have nothing to fear here; everything is in your favor.
So surrender yourself to joy; taste peace and all the other gifts of the gods, of which you will be abundantly blessed.

Tomorrow, when Dawn with her rosy fingers opens the golden gates of the east, and when the horses of the Sun, emerging from the bitter waves, spread the flames of day to chase away all the stars in the sky, we will resume, my dear Télémaque, the story of your misfortunes.

Never has your father matched your wisdom and courage: neither Achilles, conqueror of Hector, nor Theseus, returned from the underworld, nor even the great Alcides, who cleared the earth of so many monsters, have shown as much strength and virtue as you.
I wish that a deep sleep makes this night short for you.
But, alas! how long it will be for me! How I long to see you again, to hear you, to tell you again what I already know, and to ask you what I do not yet know!
Go, my dear Télémaque, with the wise Mentor, whom the gods have given you; go to that secluded cave, where everything is prepared for your rest.

I pray Morphée to spread his sweetest charms over your heavy eyelids, to let a divine vapor flow through all your tired limbs, and to send you light dreams that, fluttering around you, delight your senses with the most cheerful images, and push far away from you anything that might wake you too soon.

sentences: He showed her the letter in which his mother recounted the event, without any sentimental hypocrisy.
However, she regretted that her husband had not received the comfort of religion, having died in Doudeville, in the street, on the threshold of a café, after a patriotic meal with former officers.
Emma returned the letter; then, at dinner, out of politeness, she pretended to feel some disgust.
But as he encouraged her, she resolutely began to eat, while Charles, sitting across from her, remained motionless, in a dejected posture.
From time to time, lifting his head, he sent her a long look full of distress.
Once he sighed:
— I would have liked to see him again!
She remained silent.
Finally, realizing that she needed to speak:

And that was all.
A quarter of an hour later, he added:
— My poor mother?... what is going to become of her now?
She made a gesture of ignorance.

sentences: Indeed, the narwhal is armed with a kind of ivory sword, a halberd, according to the expression of some naturalists.
It is a main tooth that has the hardness of steel.
Some of these teeth have been found embedded in the bodies of whales that the narwhal always successfully attacks.

The museum of the Faculty of Medicine in Paris has one of these tusks that is two meters and twenty-five centimeters long and forty-eight centimeters wide at its base!

Well then! Imagine the weapon ten times stronger, and the animal ten times more powerful, launch it at a speed of twenty miles per hour, multiply its mass by its speed, and you get an impact capable of causing the requested catastrophe.

So, until further information, I would lean towards a colossal sea unicorn, armed not with a halberd, but with a true spur like armored frigates or war rams, which it would have both the mass and the driving power.

The liquid masses carry the largest known species of mammals, and perhaps they conceal mollusks of incomparable size, terrifying crustaceans to behold, such as lobsters a hundred meters long or crabs weighing two hundred tons!

"Mr. d'Épinay," he said, "I believe I need to remind you, and perhaps the timing is not as poorly chosen as one might think at first glance, because obedience to the dead is the first offering that must be placed on the coffin; I must therefore remind you of the wish expressed by Mrs. de Saint-Méran the day before yesterday on her deathbed, which is that Valentine’s marriage should not be delayed.

You know that the affairs of the deceased are perfectly in order; that her will assures Valentine the entire fortune of the Saint-Mérans; the notary showed me yesterday the documents that allow us to draft the marriage contract definitively.
You can see the notary and have him communicate these documents on my behalf.
The notary is Mr. Deschamps, located at Place Beauveau, in the Saint-Honoré suburb.
"Sir," replied d'Épinay, "it may not be the right time for Miss Valentine, as she is deep in sorrow, to think about a husband; honestly, I would be afraid....
"Valentine," interrupted Mr. de Villefort, "will have no greater desire than to fulfill her grandmother's last wishes; thus, the obstacles will not come from this side, I assure you.
"In that case, sir," replied Franz, "since they will not come from my side either, you may proceed as you wish; my word is given, and I will fulfill it, not only with pleasure but with joy.

They could hear the river flowing behind them, and occasionally, on the bank, the rustling of dry reeds.
Clumps of shadow, here and there, swelled in the darkness, and sometimes, all shivering in unison, they rose and bent like immense black waves that seemed to advance to cover them.

The cold of the night made them cling to each other more tightly; the sighs of their lips seemed louder to them; their eyes, which they could barely see, appeared larger, and in the midst of the silence, there were softly spoken words that fell on their souls with a crystalline sound and reverberated within them in multiplied vibrations.
When the night was rainy, they would take refuge in the consultation room, between the shed and the stable.
She lit one of the torches from the kitchen that she had hidden behind the books.
Rodolphe settled in there as if it were his own home.
The sight of the library and the office, of the whole apartment at last, stirred his cheerfulness; and he couldn't help making a number of jokes about Charles that embarrassed Emma.
She wished he would be more serious, and even more dramatic at times, like that one time when she thought she heard footsteps approaching in the alley.
--Someone's coming, she said...
He blew out the light.
--Do you have your pistols?
--Why?
--But... to defend yourself, Emma replied.
--Is it about your husband?
Ah! Poor boy.
And Rodolphe finished his sentence with a gesture that meant: I could crush him with a flick.
She was astonished by his bravery, although she felt a kind of indecency and naive coarseness that scandalized her.
Rodolphe thought a lot about this pistol story.

If she had been serious, it was quite ridiculous, he thought, even odious, because he had no reason to hate good Charles, not being what one calls consumed by jealousy;--and on that subject, Emma had given him quite a lecture, which he also did not find in good taste.

sentences: After conferring with Sergeant Long, Jasper Hobson decided to grant a day of rest to his companions at this location.
The actual exploration, which was meant to allow the lieutenant to identify a suitable site for establishing a trading post, was truly about to begin.
The Company had advised its agent to stay as much as possible above the seventieth parallel and along the shores of the Glacial Sea.
However, to fulfill his mandate, the lieutenant could only search to the west for a point that was as high in latitude and belonged to the American continent.

To the east, in fact, all these fragmented lands are more part of the Arctic territories, except perhaps Boothia, which is clearly cut by the seventieth parallel, but whose geographical configuration is still very uncertain.
With longitude and latitude taken, Jasper Hobson, after marking his position on the map, saw that he was still more than a hundred miles below the seventieth degree.

But beyond Cape Kruzenstern, the coast, running northeast, sharply exceeded the seventieth parallel, roughly at the one hundred thirtieth meridian, and precisely at the height of Cape Bathurst, indicated as a meeting point by Captain Craventy.
So it was this point that needed to be reached, and that is where the new fort would rise, if the location offered the necessary resources for a trading post.
"There, Sergeant Long," said the lieutenant, pointing to the map of the polar regions, "there we will be in the conditions imposed on us by the Company.
At this location, the sea, free for a large part of the year, will allow ships from the Bering Strait to reach the fort, resupply it, and export its products.
-- Not to mention," added Sergeant Long, "that since they will have established themselves beyond the seventieth parallel, our men will be entitled to double pay!
-- That goes without saying," replied the lieutenant, "and I believe they will accept it without complaint.
Well, my lieutenant, we only have to leave for Cape Bathurst now," the sergeant simply said.
However, since a day of rest was granted, the departure only took place the next day, June 6.
This second part of the journey was supposed to be and indeed was completely different from the first.
The arrangements that had governed the sledges' movement until now had not been maintained.
Each team went as it pleased.
We traveled short distances, stopped at every corner of the coast, and most often walked.

Only one recommendation had been made to his companions by Lieutenant Hobson — the recommendation not to stray more than three miles from the shore and to regroup with the detachment twice a day, at noon and in the evening.
When night fell, we camped.
The weather at that time was consistently nice, and the temperature was quite high, as it averaged fifty-nine degrees Fahrenheit above zero (15° Celsius above zero).
Two or three times, quick snowstorms broke out, but they did not last long, and the temperature was not significantly altered.

sentences: No, no!
We need to look for something else, and if we can't steer a balloon, at least we can keep it in favorable air currents.

As we ascend, these currents become much more uniform and are constant in their direction; they are no longer disturbed by the valleys and mountains that crisscross the surface of the globe, and there, as you know, lies the main cause of changes in the wind and the inconsistency of its breath.
Once these zones are determined, the balloon will only need to position itself in the currents that suit it.
But then, Commander Pennet replied, to reach them, we will have to constantly ascend or descend.
That is the real difficulty, my dear doctor.
And why is that, my dear commander?
Let's be clear: this will only be a difficulty and an obstacle for long-distance journeys, and not for simple aerial strolls.
And the reason, please?
Because you can only ascend by dropping ballast, you can only descend by losing gas, and with that maneuver, your supplies of gas and ballast will quickly be exhausted.
My dear Pennet, that is the whole question.
That is the only difficulty that science must strive to overcome.
It's not about directing the balloons; it's about moving them up and down, without using up the gas which is its strength, its lifeblood, its soul, if I may put it that way.
--You are right, my dear doctor, but this difficulty has not yet been resolved, this means has not yet been found.
--I beg your pardon, it has been found.
--By whom?
--By me!
--By you?
--You understand well that, without that, I wouldn't have risked this crossing of Africa by balloon.
After twenty-four hours, I would have run out of gas!
--But you didn't mention this in England!
No.
I didn't want to be discussed in public.
It seemed unnecessary to me.
I secretly conducted preparatory experiments, and I was satisfied; therefore, I didn't need to learn more.
--Well! my dear Fergusson, may we ask you for your secret?

sentences: At nineteen, I found my first job: a sales assistant in a small bookstore.
On the first day, I was very nervous.
I didn't know anyone and I wasn't exactly sure what my tasks were.
My boss, Madame Leroy, welcomed me with a big smile.
"Don't worry," she said to me.
Everyone starts somewhere."
She introduced me to my two colleagues, Karim and Julie, who had been working in the bookstore for several years.
At first, my tasks were simple: putting away books, helping customers, and handling the cash register.
Karim explained everything to me patiently.
When I made a mistake, he didn't make fun of me; he showed me how to do better.
The work wasn't always easy.
Some days, there were a lot of customers and I would come home tired.
But I learned something new every week, and little by little, I gained confidence.
At the end of the month, I received my first paycheck.

I invited my colleagues for a coffee to thank them.
Today, I no longer work in that bookstore.
But I will never forget that first job.
I learned an important thing there: a good boss and kind colleagues make all the difference.

sentences: What do you do for a living?
When we meet someone, this question almost always comes up first, even before we learn their name or interests.
It seems trivial, but it reveals something profound about our time: we have become accustomed to defining people, and ourselves, by our work.
It hasn't always been this way, and it's not the case everywhere.
In many cultures, people first introduce themselves by their family, village, or faith.
That work has become the default answer is therefore not obvious; it is the result of a particular history, that of societies where paid work occupies the center of existence.
This identification has its virtues.
Work structures our days, connects us to others, and gives us a sense of being useful.
Although it is often criticized, few people could stand having absolutely nothing to do.
For many, work is not just a source of income: it is a way of existing in the eyes of others.
But this same identification has a trap.
If I am only my job, what happens to my identity when I lose it — due to a layoff, an illness, or simply retirement?
Many people describe, at the moment they stop working, a feeling of emptiness, as if they had lost not just a job, but a part of themselves.
It would be naive to claim that we could entirely do without work as a reference point.
But it would be wise not to reduce our entire value to it.
A human being is also a parent, a friend, a neighbor, a curious person, a dreamer — roles that no job description mentions.
The next time we meet a stranger, we could try a different question.
Not "what do you do?", but "what are you passionate about?".
The answer, often, would tell us more about the real person.
For what we do to earn a living is just one facet of who we are.
Confusing it with the whole is to miss the essential.

sentences: I know that I know nothing.

This statement, attributed to one of the greatest sages, expresses a paradox that has traversed the entire history of thought: that the highest wisdom would begin with the awareness of one's own ignorance, and that true knowledge would include the knowledge of what one does not know.

At the end of this meditation on science and its limits, this statement deserves to be examined, as it brings together and crowns what has come before, by designating a form of knowledge superior to the accumulation of facts: the clear awareness of the extent of one's ignorance.
Let us first understand this apparent paradox.
How could the knowledge of one's ignorance be a form of wisdom, even the highest?
Isn't it better to know than not to know?
The answer lies in a distinction: between the ignorant who does not know and does not know that he does not know, and the one who, knowing much, also knows the extent of what he ignores.

The former is doubly ignorant: he is unaware, and he is unaware of his ignorance, believing himself to be knowledgeable; the latter is wiser, as he knows the limits of his knowledge and measures the extent of what escapes him.
The worst is not to be ignorant, but to be unaware that one is ignorant, to mistake one's ignorance for knowledge.
The awareness of one's ignorance is already a form of knowledge, and a valuable one: that of one's own limits.
This awareness has several virtues.

It is primarily the condition for all learning: for we only seek to know what we know we ignore; the one who believes they are knowledgeable stops learning, while the one who knows their ignorance remains open, curious, and capable of learning.
The awareness of one's ignorance is the driving force behind the desire to know, which keeps the mind active, searching, and alert.
The one who believes they know shuts themselves off; the one who knows they do not know remains open.

That is why the greatest minds have often been those who best measured the extent of their ignorance, not out of false modesty, but out of clarity: the more we know, the more we measure the vastness of what we do not know, and we discover that acquired knowledge is merely an island in an ocean of the unknown.
This awareness is also a guard against the traps of false certainty.

We have seen this regarding biases, ideology, and the limits of reason: the danger is not so much in ignorance as in believing we know what we do not know, in taking our opinions for truths, our assumptions for evidences.
The awareness of one's ignorance protects us from this presumption; it makes us cautious in our assertions, open to contradiction, and capable of recognizing our mistakes.
It is the intellectual humility without which there can be no honest thought, the remedy for dogmatism that takes its beliefs for knowledge.
Knowing that we do not know is to protect ourselves against the most dangerous of errors: the one that believes it holds the truth.
However, we must guard against a misunderstanding that would turn this wisdom into a paralyzing skepticism, a renunciation of all knowledge.
"I know that I know nothing" does not mean that we cannot know anything, that everything is equal, or that we must give up searching for the truth.
On the contrary: it is because we know the extent of our ignorance that we seek to reduce it; it is because we know our limits that we can push them back.
The awareness of one's ignorance is not a renunciation of knowledge, but its condition; it does not abolish the search for truth, it founds and animates it.
The wise person who knows they do not know is not the one who renounces knowing, but the one who knows while being aware of their limits, who seeks while knowing what eludes them.
This wisdom of ignorance crowns our journey through the highest questions.

For all these reflections on language, time, the tragic, power, beauty, and science lead to the same recognition: that the deepest knowledge includes awareness of its limits, that wisdom is not about knowing everything, but about knowing what we know and what we do not know, measuring the extent of the mystery, and remaining open to what transcends us.

Knowing that we do not know is not an admission of failure, but the highest achievement of thought: the clarity that, having learned much, measures the immensity of what remains unknown, and finds in this very measure, not discouragement, but humility, openness, and a continually renewed desire to understand.

Perhaps this is the end of all wisdom, as well as all learning: not the possession of completed knowledge, but the enlightened awareness of what we still have to learn, and the humility of one who, knowing much, knows above all how much they do not know.

sentences: He took out his watch, which he had kept to judge for himself the time that had passed.
"Half past one in the morning!" he said, "but why the devil are you waking me at this hour?"
"To tell you that you are free, Your Excellency."
"My dear," Albert replied with perfect composure, "remember this maxim of Napoleon the Great for the future: 'Only wake me for bad news.'"
If you had let me sleep, I would have finished my gallop, and I would have been grateful to you for the rest of my life....
So my ransom has been paid?
"No, Your Excellency."
"Well then, how am I free?"
"Someone, to whom I have nothing to refuse, has come to claim you."
"Until here?"
"Until here."
"Ah! by God, that someone is very kind!"
Albert looked around him and spotted Franz.
"What, is it you, my dear Franz, who takes devotion this far?" he said to him.
"No, not me," replied Franz, "but our neighbor, Mr. Count of Monte-Cristo."

"Ah indeed! Mr. Count," Albert said cheerfully as he adjusted his tie and cuffs, "you are truly a valuable man, and I hope you will consider me your eternal debtor, first for the matter of the carriage, and then for this one!" and he extended his hand to the count, who shivered at the moment of giving his own, but still did so.

sentences: I went back to Morin's place.
I found him in bed, sick with emotion and sorrow.
His wife, a tall, bony, bearded woman, was constantly mistreating him.
She introduced me into the room, shouting at me, "Are you here to see that pig Morin?
Here he is, the little rascal!"
And she stood in front of the bed, her hands on her hips.
I explained the situation; and he begged me to go find the family.
The task was delicate; however, I accepted it.
The poor guy kept repeating, "I assure you, I didn't even kiss her, no, not even.
I swear it!"
I replied, "It doesn't matter, you're just a pig."
And I took a thousand francs that he left me to use as I saw fit.
But since I didn't want to venture alone into the parents' house, I asked Rivet to accompany me.
He agreed, on the condition that we would leave immediately, because he had an urgent matter in La Rochelle the next afternoon.
And, two hours later, we were ringing the doorbell of a lovely country house.
A beautiful young girl came to open the door for us.
It was definitely her.
I whispered to Rivet, "Good heavens, I'm starting to understand Morin."
